seo.metaTitle: Convert PNG to YCbCr - Luma and Chroma Channel Map
seo.metaDescription: Split an image into luma and the two blue- and red-difference chroma channels used by video and JPEG. Free, no upload - the split runs in your browser tab.
seo.longDescription: Convert PNG to YCbCr splits the image into the color arrangement almost every video codec and JPEG uses: one brightness channel called luma, and two color-difference channels called Cb and Cr. A gray pixel is one where the color channels sit exactly at the middle value, so Cb and Cr double as a map of how much color a pixel carries rather than what color it is. The split uses the full-range weights, runs in your browser, and leaves alpha alone.
facts: Runs entirely in your browser: no upload, no server, no signup.
Y, CB or CR one at a time as grayscale, or all three as RGB.
Y is the same BT.601 luma as the grayscale tool produces.
Cb and Cr are differences: mid gray means no color, not darkness.
Free with no daily limit, no watermark and no account, also for commercial use.
howTo: Drop the image into the source area, or pick a file from your device.
Pick Component: Y for luma, CB for the blue-difference channel or CR for the red-difference channel.
Switch Display to Space as RGB to see the three parts together as red, green and blue.
Download the result from the Download button.

faq.q: Why do the Cb and Cr pictures look pale?
faq.a: Both channels sit near the middle of the range for a neutral color and drift away from it with saturation, so only the colorful parts of the image stand out from a gray background. They are differences, not colors, and half the scale is zero difference by design.

faq.q: Is Y the same as the grayscale tool?
faq.a: Yes, the weights are the same BT.601 set, so both give an identical gray picture. The difference is what comes with it: YCbCr splits the color out into two extra channels, while grayscale throws that information away.

faq.q: Can I use this to convert an image to video color?
faq.a: Not as a file. What comes out is a PNG of the channel maps, which is useful for checking a conversion by eye; to get an actual YCbCr file for a video workflow, encode it in a video or image editor.

faq.q: What do the numbers mean here?
faq.a: Each component is normalized to 0 to 1, so a neutral color reads about 0.5 in Cb and Cr. Picking one channel and viewing it in grayscale shows where that value sits relative to its extremes, bright being higher.
